explanations.answer: All their brothers plus the priests and Levites
explanations.explanation: That's the guest list, baker. David says to send word far and wide to “…the rest of our brothers in all the land of Israel, and also to the priests and Levites in their cities and pasturelands, so that they may join us.” He wants the whole nation in on this. Nobody gets left off this invite, and nobody has to hit "reply all."

Close, because the commanders are in the story. David had already conferred with them, the commanders of thousands and of hundreds, in verse 1. But the word that goes far and wide is for “…the rest of our brothers in all the land of Israel, and also to the priests and Levites…” So the invite goes way past the commanders. It's a much bigger crowd than that.

explanations.answer: The kings of the nearby nations
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't mention a single foreign king. David is speaking to the whole assembly of Israel, and he wants “…the rest of our brothers in all the land of Israel, and also to the priests and Levites in their cities and pasturelands…” to join them. This is a family gathering for Israel. I think the neighbors would've just wondered what all the noise was.

The ark it is! David says, “Then let us bring back the ark of our God…” The whole plan is about this one holy thing. Verse 6 calls it the ark of God the LORD, who is enthroned between the cherubim. Nothing about this plan is small.

An altar is a good guess for something holy, but it's not what David says. His words are, “Then let us bring back the ark of our God…” The ark is what the whole nation is going to fetch. Verse 6 says it's the ark of God the LORD, who is enthroned between the cherubim.
No tent in this plan, friend. David says, “Then let us bring back the ark of our God…” The ark is the whole reason everyone is gathering. Nobody's packing camping gear for this one.

explanations.answer: They did not inquire of God under Saul
explanations.explanation: You've got it, baker. Saul was Israel's king before David, and David says, “…for we did not inquire of Him in the days of Saul.” So the plan starts with going to God, which is the part they'd skipped. David is also asking the leaders if this is of the LORD their God (verse 2). I respect a man who checks first, because I've skipped the recipe before and learned that lesson with flour on my hat.

explanations.answer: Saul had hidden it from the people
explanations.explanation: That's a juicy story, but it's not in this passage. The text never says Saul hid anything. David's reason is that “…we did not inquire of Him in the days of Saul.” Saul was Israel's king before David. David's reason is about them, not a secret.

explanations.answer: Saul had sworn to bring it back
explanations.explanation: This passage never mentions a promise from Saul. Saul was Israel's king before David. What David says is, “…for we did not inquire of Him in the days of Saul.” That's the whole reason he gives. I'd say it's a pretty honest one.

True! The text says, “And because this proposal seemed right to all the people, the whole assembly agreed to it.” Nobody walked out and nobody stayed in their seat with their arms crossed. A whole nation on the same page is a beautiful thing. Even my cookie cutters couldn't agree on a topping.

Not false, friend. The text says, “And because this proposal seemed right to all the people, the whole assembly agreed to it.” Nobody pushed back in this passage. All the people thought it seemed right, so the whole assembly said yes.

A new cart is right! Verse 7 says, “So they carried the ark of God from the house of Abinadab on a new cart…” Brand new, not borrowed and not secondhand. Abinadab's house is where they pick the ark up. I know a thing or two about being replaced by something shinier, so I notice a new cart.

That sounds fancy, but the text doesn't say it. They carried the ark “…from the house of Abinadab on a new cart…” That's a cart, not a chariot. David is the king, and he's right there in the crowd celebrating.

No camels in this parade! The text says they carried the ark from the house of Abinadab “…on a new cart, with Uzzah and Ahio guiding the cart.” So it rolls on wheels. The oxen come up in verse 9, and they're pulling it.

Not quiet at all, baker. The text says, “David and all the Israelites were celebrating before God with all their might, with songs and on harps and lyres, with tambourines, cymbals, and trumpets.” That's a lot of noise, and nobody was whispering. You can't tiptoe past a cymbal.

False is right! The text says, “David and all the Israelites were celebrating before God with all their might, with songs and on harps and lyres, with tambourines, cymbals, and trumpets.” That's songs, strings and a full brass and percussion section. They're celebrating with all their might. Nobody on that road was using their inside voice.

explanations.answer: He takes hold of the ark
explanations.explanation: Yes, and this is where the story turns. The text says, “Uzzah reached out and took hold of the ark, because the oxen had stumbled.” Uzzah is one of the two men guiding the cart. One moment everyone is celebrating, and the next the whole parade has gone still. I think this is the part where everybody holds their breath.

explanations.answer: He jumps down to calm the oxen
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that. It says, “Uzzah reached out and took hold of the ark, because the oxen had stumbled.” Uzzah is one of the two men guiding the cart. His hand goes to the ark, not to the oxen.

explanations.answer: He shouts for everyone to stop
explanations.explanation: No shouting is mentioned. The text says, “Uzzah reached out and took hold of the ark, because the oxen had stumbled.” Uzzah is one of the two men guiding the cart. What he does is quick and silent, and it's with his hand.

Angry is right. The text says, “Then David became angry because the LORD had burst forth against Uzzah.” David even names the place Perez-uzzah. I think this one hurts, baker, because a celebration just turned into a loss. It's okay to say this is a heavy part.

The joy was in the parade, but it stopped here. The text says, “Then David became angry because the LORD had burst forth against Uzzah.” The singing and the harps came before this moment. I think this one is heavy, and it's okay to say so.

David isn't calm in this moment. The text says, “Then David became angry because the LORD had burst forth against Uzzah.” That's his reaction, plain as day. I think this is a heavy part of the story, and I'm not going to joke about it.

explanations.answer: How can I ever bring the ark of God to me
explanations.explanation: That's his question. The text says, “That day David feared God and asked, ‘How can I ever bring the ark of God to me?’” The big plan he started with now has a big question on it. I think David is thinking hard about what just happened. It's a quiet question after a very loud morning.

explanations.answer: Who will guide the cart from here on
explanations.explanation: That's a sensible question, but David doesn't ask it. The text says he “feared God and asked, ‘How can I ever bring the ark of God to me?’” His question is about the ark itself. It's about whether he can bring it at all.

explanations.answer: Where should we go to bury Uzzah
explanations.explanation: The passage never says anything about a burial. What it says is that David “feared God and asked, ‘How can I ever bring the ark of God to me?’” That's the only question David asks here. It's about the ark.

Not this time, baker. The text says, “So he did not move the ark with him to the City of David; instead, he took it aside to the house of Obed-edom the Gittite.” The City of David was the plan, but it didn't happen yet. David took it aside instead. The ark stays out of the city for now.

False is right. The text says, “So he did not move the ark with him to the City of David; instead, he took it aside to the house of Obed-edom the Gittite.” David's big plan hits a pause. The ark goes to a different house. The story isn't finished, though.

explanations.answer: The LORD blesses it and all he owns
explanations.explanation: That's the one! The text says, “Thus the ark of God remained with the family of Obed-edom in his house for three months, and the LORD blessed his household and everything he owned.” It's a good ending to a hard day. I think a blessing like that is a sweet thing to read after such a heavy moment. It's quiet and steady, and the house is full of it.

explanations.answer: His family grows afraid and leaves
explanations.explanation: The text says the opposite. The ark of God “remained with the family of Obed-edom in his house for three months.” They stayed, and “…the LORD blessed his household and everything he owned.” It's David who fears God in this passage, and Obed-edom's house is blessed.

explanations.answer: Sickness spreads all through his house
explanations.explanation: That's not what happens in this passage. The text says the ark remained with the family of Obed-edom for three months, “…and the LORD blessed his household and everything he owned.” So the story ends on a blessing, not a sickness. I think that's a relief after the last few verses.
